Sliding Window vs One Pass

The notebook's face classifier, trained on 31 × 25 crops, with its trained weights. Run it the slow way, cutting out every window of the photo and classifying each one, and the fast way, as a fully convolutional network that computes every window's answer in one pass. The two maps come out the same; time them both. Then change the scale and the threshold.

Run

The sliding window classifies the windows one at a time, row by row, and fills in the map as it goes. The times are this page's plain JavaScript; PyTorch in the notebook takes about 10 ms for the one pass and 1.4 s for the loop.

Same numbers
The fully convolutional network is the classifier with its two fully connected layers reshaped into convolutions: fc1's 64 × 768 weights become 64 filters of 32 × 6 × 4. On one 31 × 25 crop it computes exactly what the classifier computes; on a bigger photo it computes it for every window 4 pixels apart.

    
Why one pass is faster
Neighboring windows overlap almost entirely, so the sliding window recomputes nearly the same convolutions thousands of times. One pass computes each convolution once for the whole photo and shares it among all the windows that need it.

    
Scale matters
The classifier only knows faces about 31 pixels tall. At scales 0.8 and 0.9 it finds all five faces; at 0.6 and at 1.0 only three of them, and not the same three. A real detector runs over a pyramid of scales and merges the overlapping boxes (Lecture 16).
